explanation: Traditional moko was carved into the skin with chisels called uhi, leaving grooves rather than a smooth surface. The English word tattoo comes from Polynesian tatau.

claims.text: Tā moko is the traditional tattoo art of the Māori of New Zealand (Aotearoa).
Tā moko is not the tattoo tradition of Samoans, Native Hawaiians or the Inuit.
Traditional tā moko was carved into the skin with chisels called uhi, leaving grooved skin.
The English word tattoo comes from the Polynesian word tatau.

evidence.restatement: Tā moko is the traditional tattooing of the Māori of New Zealand.
Samoans, Native Hawaiians and the Inuit have tattoo traditions of their own; tā moko is Māori.
Traditional moko was cut with uhi, bone chisels, leaving grooved skin rather than a smooth surface.
English 'tattoo' comes from Polynesian tatau, recorded on Cook's 1769 voyage.

Samoans have the pe'a and malu, Native Hawaiians kākau, the Inuit kakiniit; none of those is tā moko.
